name: Okpamheri

catalog_locator: Elugbe 1989 sec. 4.17.8 'Tone' (Ibilo), p.95; sec. 4.16.8 'Tone' (Emhalhe/Somorika), pp.92-93; ch.2 sec. 2.2.4 'Other vowel features', p.43; Elugbe 1973 sec. 6 'Tone' (Ibilo), pp.263-265.
catalog_quote: [Elugbe 1989 sec. 4.17.8 Tone, p.95, Ibilo] Ibilo exhibits a 'two tone plus downstep' system. There is no evidence of synchronic downdrifting in my data, although Akinlabi (1979) rather routinely claimed downdrift exists in Ibilo. ... The downstep in Ibilo is limited in occurrence and is unlikely to be successfully analysed as a 'mid' tone. [sec. 4.16.8 Tone, pp.92-93, Emhalhe (Somorika)] I do not know of any other Edoid language with greater complexity of tone (at least on the surface) than is found in Emhalhe. It would appear that three levels are distinctive and the mid level is not to be interpreted as a downstep. ... Laniran (1981) also tackles the problem of Emhalhe tone, and confirms some observations of mine: in nouns as lexical items, initial lows become high-falling while final non-lows are realized with a fall. [ch.2 sec. 2.2.4, p.43] Final devoicing of vowels has been observed in Ibilo by Akinlabi (1979). It is a feature that I have confirmed elsewhere and its effect is to shorten final vowels in stems of two (or, rarely, more) syllables. ... the final vowels are decidedly shorter than the non-final ones. ... We may refer to this process as vowel weakening in final position.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Okpamheri (described through its Ibilo and Emhalhe/Somorika varieties) is analysed purely as a level-tone language: Ibilo has two tones (H, L) plus a restricted non-automatic downstep, with four lexical tone classes on disyllabic nouns (LL, LH, HL, HH) and grammatical tone in the verb phrase; Emhalhe has three distinctive levels. Neither Elugbe 1973 nor Elugbe 1989 (nor any other opened source) mentions word stress or accent at all; the only prominence-adjacent remark is Elugbe 1989:43 that stem-final vowels of disyllabic stems in Ibilo and Emhalhe are shortened and partly devoiced ('vowel weakening in final position').
new_statements.exceptions: none regarding stress; tonal notes only (LL nouns surface high-falling-low in isolation in Ibilo; in Emhalhe initial lows become high-falling and final non-lows are realized with a fall in citation nouns).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on nouns in citation form and completive (N+N) phrases; grammatical tone in verb phrases. No stress domain defined because stress is never discussed. Statements are for the Ibilo (Ibillo town) and Emhalhe (Somorika) varieties, both subsumed under okpa1238.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand phonology is for particular varieties now subsumed under okpa1238: Ibilo = Okpamheri of Ibillo town (retired ISO [ibi], Glottolog bookkeeping ibil1238; Elugbe 1973 pp.241-265, 1989 sec. 4.17) and Emhalhe = Somorika (Elugbe 1989 sec. 4.16; Elugbe lists 'Emhalhe (Somorika)' as a unit coordinate with 'Okpamheri' in his 1989 classification p.24, but calls both Ibilo and Emhalhe 'Okpamheri dialects' in his 1989 Edoid chapter p.298; Blench 2020 and Glottolog treat Emhalhe as a division of Okpamheri). Decker et al. 2024 data are the Uma variety (Imoga, Aduge = retired [adu], adug1238). Lewis (2004, 2015) argues Okpamheri has split into four languages (Ibilo, Aiyegunle, Dagbala..). Tone systems differ by variety (Ibilo 2 tones + downstep; Emhalhe 3 levels).
